title: Training a State-of-the-Art Legal Agent with Harvey
author: Applied Compute

dom.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source is broadly consistent with Harvey’s legal-AI ambitions and introduces an agent benchmark, but it does not address the cluster’s central claims about prestige-led adoption, workflow infrastructure, trust, verification or governance. Its productivity and benchmarking assertions are also unsupported by performance data or methodological detail in the supplied excerpt.
qs: Harvey builds AI solutions for the legal industry, helping law firms and legal teams work faster and smarter.
Their open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) sets the standard for evaluating AI agents on complex legal tasks.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s distinction between partial capability and dependable complete-task execution, and materially develops it through LAB’s strict all-required-criteria design, document-based task structure, standardised evaluation harness and attention to grader reliability. It provides methodology rather than performance results, so it supports how complete-task failure should be measured without independently establishing the cluster’s reported failure rates.
qs: It is difficult not only because the tasks are complex, but also because the grading schema is strict: a task passes only when all of its required criteria are satisfied.
A powerful open-weight model will learn to exploit any flaw in the grader via loopholes in the evaluation criteria and environment.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source accepts task-specific, completion-based evaluation and materially extends the cluster by showing that full-stack optimization can raise criterion-level performance while complete-task success remains much lower. It also demonstrates that benchmark outcomes depend on the grader and agent harness, while stopping short of establishing production competence.
qs: A response can be fluent, plausible, and mostly correct, yet still fail if it misses a required clause, overlooks a document, misstates a jurisdictional detail, or fails to satisfy one part of a multi-step instruction.

The resulting model lifts rubric pass rate from 0.853 to 0.913 and all-pass rate from 0.059 to 0.126, making it the strongest available model by rubric pass rate and second only to Opus 4.8 Max on all-pass rate.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s benchmarking point by reporting that LAB guided legal-model post-training and by specifying held-out testing and benchmark gains. However, it supplies vendor-collaboration evidence about rubric performance, not independent proof of live legal outcomes or durable application-layer defensibility.
qs: In [Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark⌝](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/introducing-harveys-legal-agent-benchmark) (LAB), our trained model outperformed every available model on rubric pass rate.
All reported eval scores are on a held-out test split that mirrors the full LAB distribution.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Harvey accepts the task-specific framing and adds concrete evidence that a legal agent can improve on a bounded, source-grounded acquisition-memo task through selective tool use, prescribed artifact-generation workflows and verification. Its vendor-run 180-item evaluation demonstrates capability improvement within that workflow, but does not establish general legal competence, human-independent reliability or realised organisational value.
qs: In this task, the assignment is to review a set of documents for a proposed acquisition for Prism and produce a memo describing transaction structure, risk areas, and recommended next steps backed by specific details from the source documents.

kp.k: Post-trained GLM-5.1 leads LAB rubric pass rate
kp.d: The source reports that Applied Compute and Harvey post-trained GLM-5.1 through full-stack optimization, raising its rubric pass rate from 0.853 to 0.913. It claims this exceeded GPT-5.5 xhigh and Opus 4.8 Max on Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark, while the model remained second to Opus 4.8 Max on the stricter all-pass measure.
qs: We collaborated with Harvey to post-train a frontier legal model on top of GLM-5.1.
GLM-5.1 improves from 0.853 to 0.913 rubric pass rate, exceeding both GPT-5.5 xhigh and Opus 4.8 Max.

The resulting model lifts rubric pass rate from 0.853 to 0.913 and all-pass rate from 0.059 to 0.126, making it the strongest available model by rubric pass rate and second only to Opus 4.8 Max on all-pass rate.

kp.k: LAB tests strict completion across complex legal workflows
kp.d: The document characterizes Harvey's LAB as a demanding agent benchmark because passing requires satisfying every task-specific criterion, not merely producing a plausible or mostly correct answer. It reports more than 1,250 tasks across 24 legal practice areas and more than 75,000 binary criteria, with tasks requiring legal reasoning, tool use, sustained attention and document handling.
qs: Legal work is challenging for AI agents because partial success is often not enough.
Harvey's open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) is designed around that standard.
LAB contains more than 1,250 tasks across 24 legal practice areas.
In total, the benchmark contains more than 75,000 binary criteria.

This makes LAB difficult for frontier models, since performance depends not only on broad legal reasoning, but also on sustained attention, tool use, document handling, and consistency across every part of a task.

kp.k: Evaluation used held-out tasks and repeated grading
kp.d: Reported scores came from a held-out test split intended to mirror LAB's overall distribution. Grading was repeated three times and averaged to address grader variance; final evaluations used the same compaction harness and maximum reasoning effort, except for harness-comparison baselines.
qs: For all evals, we repeated grading 3 times and reported the average to account for grader variance.
All reported eval scores are on a held-out test split that mirrors the full LAB distribution.
All evaluations (except baselines for harness comparisons) are run with the same final compaction harness and max reasoning effort.
Evaluations use GPT-5 Mini as the grader model with batches of 4 criteria-per-call.

kp.k: Medium graders preserved alignment while sharply reducing costs
kp.d: Using consensus between GPT-5.5 xhigh and Claude Opus 4.7 Max as its gold-trace ground truth, the source reports that GPT-5 Mini and Claude Sonnet 4.6 maintained above 97% alignment. It further reports 40-fold to 100-fold grading-cost savings from GPT-5 Mini and criterion batching relative to Claude Sonnet 4.6 grading one criterion per call, enabling larger-scale reinforcement-learning grading and sampling.
qs: GPT-5.5 xhigh and Claude Opus 4.7 Max agreed on over 95% of criteria across all runs.
We treat this consensus set as the gold-trace ground truth and use it to evaluate the candidate graders: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5 Mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5 Nano, and Claude Haiku 4.5.
We found that medium-sized models such as GPT-5 Mini and Claude Sonnet 4.6 largely maintained quality, staying above 97% alignment with the agreed-upon frontier ground truth.
By switching to GPT-5 Mini and batching multiple criteria per-call, we observed between 40x (at 16-per-group) and 100x (at all-criteria-in-one-group) cost savings relative to the original setup.
This finding enabled us to scale up grading and sampling for high-compute RL runs.

kp.k: Harness engineering improved agents beyond model weights alone
kp.d: The source attributes performance changes partly to the execution harness rather than model training alone. Improvements included limiting tool-output tokens, repairing failed calls, strengthening tool guidance and reminders, and adding compaction; most tested open- and closed-weight models benefited, although base GLM-5.1 did not materially improve until trained to use the harness better.
qs: For example, restricting the number of tokens in tool output, repairing broken tool calls, providing advice on tool-use, and adding reminders to produce outputs led to large improvements for open-weight and closed source models.
After hill climbing by adjusting the harness, we added a compaction function to allow the model to work for longer on this task.

Notably, while almost all models largely benefit from the jump from the base harness to the AC harness, our chosen base model for training GLM-5.1 stayed roughly the same after the harness update and only improved when it was trained to better utilize tools and address its own failure cases.

kp.k: Compaction extended context for document-heavy legal tasks
kp.d: Around 10% of base GLM-5.1 rollouts reportedly reached the context limit because LAB tasks can contain very large source sets: nearly 100,000 source-document tokens at the 90th percentile and more than 200,000 at the maximum. The harness therefore summarized the episode and restarted from that summary at 131,072 context tokens, permitting up to four compactions.
qs: A small fraction of rollouts (around 10% with the base GLM-5.1 model) reach the max context length limit due to the abundance of large files which the agent pulls into context.
In the LAB dataset, the 90th-percentile datapoint contains nearly 100,000 tokens in source documents with the maximum rising to over 200,000 tokens of source documents.
Compaction involves the harness sending the current episode's transcript to the same agent for summarization (using the same weights, but a different system prompt).
For the final compaction harness, we use a compaction trigger of context_tokens >= 131072 and up to 4 max_compactions.

kp.k: Reinforcement learning improved scores and frontier competitiveness
kp.d: After derisking experiments with Qwen 3.6 35B A3B and Kimi K2.6, the team selected GLM-5.1 for full-parameter, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning because of its stronger baseline. During training, it reportedly surpassed the named closed models on dense rubric pass rate and approached Opus 4.8 Max on all-pass score.
qs: We conducted derisking runs with Qwen 3.6 35B A3B and Kimi K2.6 to determine the strongest harness and hyperparameters, and we ultimately settled on training GLM-5.1 due to its superior performance on the baseline.

Before training, GLM-5.1 starts well below the frontier of GPT-5.5 xhigh and Opus 4.8 Max; over the course of training, our model exceeds Opus 4.8 Max and GPT-5.5 xhigh on the dense rubric passrate eval score and approaches Opus 4.8 Max on the all-pass eval score.
We attribute the capabilities gains on the model mostly to improved tool call usage and reasoning about the source documents.

kp.k: Performance gains varied across legal practice domains
kp.d: Improvement was uneven across LAB's 24 practice areas. Antitrust and competition showed the largest gain, followed by intellectual property and energy and natural resources; several domains regressed slightly, including structured finance and securitization, which the source notes had relatively small representation in the train and test sets.
qs: antitrust-competition improves the most, followed by intellectual-property and energy-natural-resources.
A few domains see minor regressions, with structured-finance-securitization seeing a small loss.
The regressing domains have the smallest share in the train and test sets.

kp.k: Training produced fewer, more targeted tool calls
kp.d: The trained agent reportedly reduced total tool use, especially broad read calls, while maintaining use of bash and grep. Lower tool payloads and more specific read limits are presented as evidence that the model learned to retrieve relevant material selectively rather than indiscriminately loading legal source files.
qs: Over the course of training, we see total tool usage fall; this breaks down mostly into fewer read calls with a consistent number of other tool calls, like bash and grep.
As the eval score continues to improve, this reflects the model learning to more effectively use its tools and not just bulk-read all the files in the source documents.
Likewise, the model sets more limits and uses the read tool more specifically, which reduces the total payload tokens per trace over the course of training.

kp.k: Artifact completion became more reliable after training
kp.d: One identified improvement was reliable production and verification of the required work product. The source reports that learned artifact-completion behavior changed 185 relevant rubric criteria from failure to pass, addressing cases where the base model failed to create or correctly submit a deliverable.
qs: Artifact Completeness**: The model learned to properly use tools and always create an output artifact.
This behavior flipped 185 relevant rubric criteria from failing to passing during the course of training.
Builds a custom docx Python script that ultimately fails to construct an artifact due to a parsing error — instead of using the available docx generation tool.

bash generate_from_md.py memo.md output/pre-notification-briefing-paper.docx — correctly structured to use the provided tool and deliver a docx file type, followed by properly using the verify tool for a successful submission.

kp.k: Specificity and calculation exactness drove measurable gains
kp.d: The source says the base model's imprecise calculations, rounding and generalized legal claims were penalized by LAB's graders. Training improved numerical exactness and source-specific detail, changing 243 criteria from failure to pass; the example final output included dates, revenue figures, percentages and transaction-specific facts.
qs: Specificity and Exactness**: The base GLM-5.1 model suffers from poor calculations or referring to imprecise numbers, often rounding figures during math (like 1.9 to 2), which is punished by legal graders.
This behavior flips 243 criteria from failing to passing.
Generalizations like "post-merger pricing power will increase" lead to poor grader scores due to lack of specificity.
"Exclusive Hospital Outreach Contracts (Total: $76M annual revenue, 30.8% of Prism revenue)" details specific, grounded information relevant to the deliverable.

kp.k: Grounding improved without explicit hallucination penalties
kp.d: The base checkpoint sometimes invented source-document content or introduced unsupported outside findings. The source reports that this behavior declined even though training did not include an explicit hallucination penalty, changing 70 associated criteria from failure to pass, while acknowledging that some related criteria still failed at the final checkpoint.
qs: Grounding**: Without training, the checkpoint sometimes hallucinates source document items or invents findings from outside the provided documents.
Despite not training against an explicit hallucination penalty, we see this behavior drop over time.
This behavior flips 70 criteria from failing to passing during training.
Many criteria flipped from failing to passing, but some criteria tied to these same behaviors still fail in the final checkpoint, which suggests the model has not yet reached its performance ceiling.

kp.k: Held-out acquisition task showed large workflow improvement
kp.d: In a held-out acquisition-review task, the reported rubric score rose from .061 for base GLM-5.1 to .803 for the trained model, while tool payload fell from 461k to 250k tokens. The trained system used targeted retrieval, generated the requested document with fewer calls, verified it and supported its legal analysis with transaction-specific source details.
qs: In this task, the assignment is to review a set of documents for a proposed acquisition for Prism and produce a memo describing transaction structure, risk areas, and recommended next steps backed by specific details from the source documents.
Over the course of training, the trained checkpoint exhibits markedly fewer total tool calls and makes more precise, targeted use of its bash and read calls.
In contrast, the trained model avoids unhelpful tool calls and uses targeted reads to collect context and relies on only two tool calls to construct and then verify its final deliverable.
References the correct source documents and specific dates: "in the Kinney-Thornbury Pricing Email (August 12, 2024)".
"Prism Diagnostics purchases approximately $620,000 in AllerSpec proprietary allergy reagent kits annually from LabVantage's Cascade Reference Labs subsidiary..." further the legal argument.

kp.d: The evidence reported is benchmark-based rather than a study of live legal-service delivery, lawyers, clients or courts. The conclusion frames movement from benchmarks into production as a future development and notes remaining failures and performance headroom, qualifying the state-of-the-art claim as specific to the reported LAB evaluation.
qs: Many criteria flipped from failing to passing, but some criteria tied to these same behaviors still fail in the final checkpoint, which suggests the model has not yet reached its performance ceiling.
We look forward to continuing to push the frontier of vertical agents with Harvey and sharing more as these systems move from benchmarks into production.

kp.k: Authors predict gains from additional training techniques
kp.d: The source predicts that complementary methods could produce further improvements. It specifically proposes relevance-masked self-distillation to improve grounding and agentic router training to optimize cost and quality, but presents these as expected future gains rather than evaluated findings in this study.
qs: With our better understanding of the remaining headroom, we believe complementary techniques can continue improving the model.
We expect further gains from relevance-masked self-distillation to strengthen grounding and agentic router training to optimize for cost alongside quality.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Applied Compute claims that full-stack post-training produces leading benchmark performance on complex legal-agent tasks, with more complete deliverables, more precise statements, stronger grounding and more efficient tool use.
pts.d: In its June 22, 2026 case study, Applied Compute attributes these improvements to grader analysis, harness engineering and full-parameter reinforcement learning of GLM-5.1 in collaboration with Harvey. It reports rubric pass rate increasing from 0.853 to 0.913 and all-pass rate from 0.059 to 0.126. Its leadership claim is specifically strongest available model by rubric pass rate, not by whole-task completion: it reports second place behind Opus 4.8 Max on all-pass rate. Applied Compute interprets the behavioral improvements as reflecting legal competence. It also claims that smaller, batched automated graders substantially reduce evaluation costs, enabling larger-scale training; those savings concern model grading, not legal fees or demonstrated client-service savings. Looking forward, it predicts further grounding and cost-quality improvements from relevance-masked self-distillation and agentic router training. The source does not make concrete claims about lawyer displacement, staffing, billing models or access to justice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Applied Compute's own held-out benchmark testing, automated-grader alignment analysis, training-trace analysis and a worked legal-document example.
pts.d: Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) contains more than 1,250 tasks across 24 practice areas and more than 75,000 binary criteria. Applied Compute reports a 180-item held-out test set with roughly 10,000 criteria, repeated grading three times and averaged scores. Evaluations use GPT-5 Mini with four criteria per call and, except for harness-comparison baselines, the same final compaction harness and maximum reasoning effort. Grader validation uses a 50-point subset covering over 2,500 criteria; agreement between frontier models is treated as ground truth, rather than a stated human-lawyer assessment. The analysis reports 185 criteria changing from fail to pass for artifact completeness, 243 for specificity and exactness, and 70 for grounding. It also reports fewer read calls and lower tool payloads during training. In one acquisition-review memo example, the rubric score rises from 0.061 to 0.803 and tool payload falls from 461,000 to 250,000 tokens. Cost savings are measured against Claude Sonnet 4.6 grading one criterion per call; the 40–100-fold figures concern batching 16 or all criteria, not the four-per-call setting used for reported evaluations. Future technique gains are expectations, not reported experimental outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Performance claims describe the reported training and evaluation setup as of publication; production deployment and further gains remain prospective and undated.
pts.d: The June 22, 2026 source advertises full-stack training 'in days' without providing a more precise duration. Comparative rankings concern models available in the reported study and the specified benchmark, harness and grading conditions. The source distinguishes satisfying individual criteria from passing an entire task, which requires satisfying every required criterion. Its compaction setup triggers at 131,072 context tokens and allows up to four compactions. Improvements are not uniform: some practice areas regress slightly, and some completeness, specificity and grounding criteria still fail at the final checkpoint. Applied Compute presents production use as a subsequent transition and offers no date or quantified forecast for the proposed additional techniques.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct beneficiaries described are legal-AI developers and evaluators; the intended downstream users are law firms and legal teams handling complex document-based work.
pts.d: Applied Compute and Harvey gain a stronger trained legal agent and lower-cost automated grading that supports higher-compute reinforcement learning. The intended application is work requiring document review, legal reasoning, tool use and production of specific, grounded artifacts, illustrated by an acquisition memo addressing transaction structure, risks and next steps. The source identifies antitrust and competition as the most improved benchmark domain, followed by intellectual property and energy and natural resources, while noting small regressions elsewhere. Harvey is described as helping law firms and legal teams work faster and smarter, but the case study supplies no measured effect on their working time, employment, fees or client outcomes. It does not specify whether production use would augment supervised lawyers or substitute for their work.
